title: My Plan to Never Get Alzheimer's Disease
description: When I was just 23 years old, I was handed a terrible verdict. I learned that I carried not just one copy but two copies of a genetic variant ( ApoE4/4 ) that dramatically increased my chances of developing Alzheimer’s disease, raising my risk by 12- to 15-fold. The great irony is that I received this news while I was pursuing my PhD studying neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. I knew exactly what this diagnosis meant, and I had already seen firsthand the devastation these diseases cause. My initial reaction was more than anxiety; it was terror. But I used that as fuel to dig deeper into the research. Now, seven years later, after earning a PhD in metabolism, completing medical school, and spending nearly a decade obsessively studying the science of brain health, I have something I didn’t have back then. I have tools. And most importantly, I have hope. In this letter, I’ll show you where the science stands, the specific tools I use , and the exciting future that’s coming next… *Author’s Note: A branching ecosystem of information A lot of what I write is dense, so I’m trying something a little more accessible with this letter. It’s self-contained, but also serves as a branching ecosystem of information. Wherever you see an asterisk (*), you’ll find a link to a separate 3,000- to 7,000-word deep dive for those who want to explore further. Lifestyle: A Clone Thought Experiment I want to begin with lifestyle. But rather than present you with a dry list, let me start with a thought experiment. Imagine I cloned myself, right down to the two copies of ApoE4 that supposedly sealed my brain’s fate. Then imagine those two versions of me walked off in opposite directions and lived out the next fifty years. In 50 years, one of us has Alzheimer’s.

title: I've Been Using Olive Oil Wrong for Years
description: I just learned I’ve been eating olives wrong for years. And my olive oil game needed a tune-up too. But let’s start with the whole olive. Here’s the deal: I’ve been an olive oil obsessive for the better part of a decade. I’ve also learned how to pick my olive oils. But I didn’t know olives themselves had a problem. Most olives in the United States are cured in a chemical called lye. Lye is sodium hydroxide, a very harsh chemical. Producers use it to de-bitter olives more quickly. But this strips the olives of many of their critical nutrients, such that they no longer retain the same health benefits as fresh or properly fermented olives. The natural curing process, which creates an organic olive, takes far longer. Rather than a few days, it can take 6 to 12 months. There are olives you can buy using this process, but it’s not necessarily obvious which are which. I’ll tell you precisely which olives I use later. And they’re not only healthier because of their wider range of nutrients and their probiotic properties, but they also taste phenomenally better. But first, let’s rewind. Because are olives and olive oil even worth the hype? In a word: Yes. But not because they’re healthy fats. Think of olive oil like a delicious soup. Technically, most of the soup might be water, but calling it healthy water would completely miss the point. The same is true of olive oil.

title: How to Recharge Your Body’s Antioxidants
description: Every cell in your body carries a rechargeable battery for fighting oxidative stress. It’s called glutathione. Every time it neutralizes a free radical, the glutathione battery drains. And how well your cells recharge it may matter as much as how much of it you have. Now, emerging literature on glutathione shows promise for use cases ranging from reducing wrinkles (yes, mom, don’t worry, I got you) to Parkinson’s disease to liver health. Today, we’ll look at what happens when you top it up from the outside, and at a surprising way to keep the charger running from the inside. What Is Glutathione? Glutathione is a molecule your body naturally produces in virtually every cell. Structurally, it’s made from three amino acids (glutamate, cysteine, and glycine). And functionally, I call it the cell’s “rechargeable battery” for handling oxidative and chemical stress. What do I mean by that? Glutathione can donate electrons to neutralize reactive oxygen species . These are free radicals that can damage proteins, fats, and DNA. I n the process, two glutathione molecules link together to form an oxidized version called GSSG. Then, another enzyme uses energy from a different molecule, NADPH , to convert GSSG back into the active form of glutathione, effectively “recharging” the glutathione battery to be used again. We’ll come back to that recycling system later. I promise. But that’s only one of glutathione’s jobs. Second , glutathione helps recharge other antioxidants, including vitamin C and E. So rather than acting alone, glutathione sits at the hub of an antioxidant network. And third , glutathione plays a central role in detoxification, particularly in the liver.
